paragraphs.text: BY OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS [CYRIL], ARCHBISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, AGAINST THE ANTHROPOMORPHITES: LETTER TO CALOSYRIUS. Some people who had come from the mountain of Calamon were asked by me about the monks there: how they spend their days, and what manner of life they follow. They said that many are highly regarded for their ascetic discipline, and that the monks earnestly wish to achieve a [?] life. But there are some, they said, who go about and, out of ignorance, disturb those who wish to live quietly. Then these people make up stories, asserting [?] … A most learned man, both a philosopher and [?] … the beginning of the third book [?]. The Audians, or Odians, are an order. They make their dwelling in monasteries, withdrawing as an order both into deserts and nearer to cities, in suburbs, and wherever they have their own dwellings, or sheepfolds.

such things. For they said: "Since divine Scripture says that man came into being according to the image of God, we must believe that the Divine is human-shaped, that is, has a human form." This is utterly senseless, and it can make those who choose to think this way liable to charges of the most extreme impiety. Man is indeed made according to the image of God, as everyone agrees, but the likeness is not bodily, for God is incorporeal. The Saviour himself teaches this when he says, "God is spirit." So if he is spirit, he does not have a body, nor does he have the form of a body. For what lies outside body would lie outside shape as well, since the Divine has no quantity and no shape. But if they think that the God who is over all was himself shaped after the nature of the human body, let them say whether he too has feet so that he can walk, hands so that he can work with them, and eyes so that he can see with them. Where, then, does he go? From what places does he pass to what places, he who fills all things? For he said, "Do I not fill heaven and earth?" Or what hands does he set in motion to work, he who creates through his living Word? And if he has eyes as we do, set in a face, then he certainly cannot see what is behind him. When he looks to the east, he does not know what the people in the west are doing, and when he looks back to the west, he does not see those in the east. I am ashamed even to write these things, but because of some people's folly I have become a fool. I did not do so willingly; rather, they forced me. So let those who babble such things be silenced as ignorant. Let them stop meddling in what is beyond their power and keep quiet, or rather, let them stop speaking against God. For God is above all creation. He is not to be thought of as a body, nor in bodily outlines or shapes. He is simple, immaterial, formless and uncompounded, not put together from parts or limbs or members as we are. Rather, as the Scriptures say, he is spirit. He oversees all things, is everywhere, fills all things and is absent from nothing, for he fills heaven and earth. That man was made according to the image of God has other meanings and senses. For of all the living creatures on earth, he alone is rational and compassionate, and has an aptitude for every virtue, having been allotted … [?] [Here the text is interrupted by an editor's note:] … sets out: "For [they think] the human-shaped [?] …" … [?] fools [?] … but he adds [?] … "Since they entangle themselves in what was said by way of condescension, and cannot bear to conceive anything more divine" [?] … "they do the better thing, those who [?] the better part of man" … "those who portray the Divine in the better part of man," where "the better" is expressly explained [?] … "they swear by the greater," where by the great[er] [?] …

[the soul] is rational, and because it loves virtue and rules over the things on earth, man is said to have been made in the image of God. But if they think that the image is meant in terms of the shape of the body … NOTES OF BONAVENTURA VULCANIUS. … in whom there is more good sense, while another has a lack of wits, and still others are out of their minds. For the mind is truly one and the same; it comes from God [?] and has been given equally to all human beings. "Let us make man," he says, "according to our image and likeness." Nevertheless, such a mind shows its activities according to how its organ is formed (the organ of the mind is the brain). This visible sun was created by the Creator as the brightest of things, so that from there it might light up the whole region around the earth with its boundless [?]; and yet it sends its rays down to us according to how thin or thick the air is. In the same way our mind shows its activity according to the quality of its organ. The radiance of our mind is overshadowed by this fleshly thickness, as the sun is by a cloud, and our condition afterwards shows this plainly [?], so that today one person surpasses another in reason and understanding. So do not object to this, and do not accuse the Creator because of the inequality. Such inequality has secured equal rights for everyone. For if this were [?], most people would not have been brought into subjection, and the foolish would not have submitted, willingly or unwillingly, to the wise. Nature does these things by its own course, as the great Basil said: "[?] by a command spoken at the beginning of creation, it advances through all things [?] … to what is said [?]." At the beginning God said, "Let the earth bring forth vegetation." From that time on the earth has never stopped conceiving plants every year and bringing them to birth, as though it remembered that voice. Even if it heard the voice [only once?], it has naturally kept on doing its work ever since, and doing it intelligently. Where the earth is rocky, hard and resistant, it is wholly unfruitful and unfit for its work, but where it is rich and fertile, a multitude of plants springs up. The same thing can be seen in a woman's womb. God said, "Increase and multiply," and so, as husband and wife come together, the human race increases [?]. But wherever a womb is found to be badly tempered, it is wholly barren and quite unsuited to bearing children. This, then, is how we should understand the question before us. God did say, "Let us make man according to our image" (and the image of God, as was said above, is our mind). Nevertheless, the mind shows its activity according to the condition of its organ. So when the organ is in its natural state, the mind also works according to nature, [?] but when the organ is damaged in any way, the mind too becomes unfit for its activities, even if in itself it suffers no change [?]. You can see this with a harpist and his harp. The tuning of the instrument often goes off, but the craftsman's skill is in no way impaired. Consider that exactly the same thing happens with our mind and with the organ through which it normally acts. So the mind is the same in all people, after the likeness of the sun, because it was constituted through the divine breath. The organs, however, differ, since they are composed of the four elements, and the mind acts in accordance with them. Do not be surprised at this any further. As was said, it was very much to our advantage that at the beginning God allowed the four elements to come together and to make up this earthly man. This is where the difference in our bodies comes from, as [?] …

image, then nothing prevents us from saying that God also has the same form as the irrational animals. For we see that they too are made of the same parts as we are: they have feet and eyes, nostrils and a tongue, and the other members of the body. So let your Piety stop such people, or rather rebuke those who are in the habit of babbling such things. I hear that they say the mystical eulogia is of no use for sanctification if a remnant of it is kept for another day … [?] … that all should be recognized by one another. For our mind does not now have a power of discernment so sound that it can grasp all things without distinguishing marks. If everyone had one and the same appearance, life would fall into no ordinary confusion. So divine Providence, coming to the aid of our weaknesses, allowed differences between bodies to arise from the way the elements are mixed. This is why some people are intelligent and others unintelligent, some strong and others weak, some bold and others timid. This is why some people are sickly and others are not, some long-lived and others short-lived. And this is what the great Cyril said: "After the fall, God allowed each person to live out their life according to whatever temperament they happened to have." Why did God allow these things to happen at the beginning? First, so that people might remember that former way of life and so lament their own ill counsel [?]. Second, so that everything might be carried on in some order and rhythm, with some ruling and others being ruled, and so that no one would be puffed up against another because of equality. If this is how things are, do not pry any further into the divine [wisdom] [?] … for it is unsearchable. And the inequality that seems so to the many paradoxically gives equal rights to all.

(5) "I hear that they say the mystical eulogia is of no use for sanctification." On this mystical [eulogia] [?] … I [hear?], beloved, that some people, carried away by their own reasoning, have no small doubts about the nature of the spotless mysteries of Christ. Sometimes they call it incorruptible, since it bestows immortal life; at other times they insist that it is corruptible, since it is consumed by our teeth and eaten. [?] They try to say a great deal on their own authority, but it seems they play thoughtlessly in matters that are not for play, and laugh at things that are not to be laughed at, and so are led on to dangerous ground. But do not be like them, beloved, and busy yourself with the divine mysteries. Do not trust in yourself and leap beyond the set bounds, prying into whether the holy communion of Christ is above corruption or is merely temporary. Such things are [not] worth examining. However, [accept] the one view as pious, and do not accept the other as impious [?]. For if you examine the meaning of the matter thoroughly, you will find both in this communion. The bread of the offering is that very flesh of Christ, [crucified?] and given over to burial. This is clear from what the Lord himself said to the disciples when he was instituting the mysteries of the New Covenant. As he gave them these, he said: "Take, eat; this is my body, broken for you for the forgiveness of sins." Pay attention, then. If the Lord's flesh had not been corruptible, it would not have been subject to [?] corruption, for what is incorruptible is beyond all corruption. In the same way the bread of the offering is also subject to corruption, since it is flesh …

… day. But they are out of their minds to say these things. For Christ is not altered, nor will his holy body be changed. Rather, the power of the blessing and the life-giving grace remain in it perpetually. Some others too, they say, go about (6) pretending to devote themselves to prayer alone. They do no work, and they make piety a pretext for idleness and profit. Their thinking is not right. If it were, they would have to call themselves better than the holy apostles, who worked whenever circumstances gave them time for it, and also toiled for the word of God. And how have they forgotten that the blessed Paul wrote to some people: "For I hear that some among you are walking about, not working at all, but being busybodies"? So the Church does not approve of those who do this. Admittedly, those who live quietly in ascetic dwellings must pray earnestly. But working does no harm; rather, it is extremely beneficial. Then a person will not be found a burden to others by living off their sweat for his own needs, and from his own labour he will be able to comfort a widow and an orphan, and some of the brothers who are sick. But if they think it a good thing not to touch any work, then when everyone imitates them, who will feed them? NOTES OF BONAVENTURA VULCANIUS. [?] … when they are about to [depart], if they happen to partake of the holy mysteries of Christ with a pure conscience, they are led away escorted by angels, and for that reason surely [?] … But see here too God's love for humanity. Since the many-wiled dragon brought destruction upon us through tasting, the means of healing has again been devised through tasting. So those who in any way keep themselves far from the holy communion of Christ cannot be among the living at all. The Lord showed this when he said: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you." So let us purify ourselves and approach the spiritual table. In this way, having become partakers of immortal food, we shall attain [?] in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen. (6) "Some others go about." [?] …

Some people make it an excuse for idleness and gluttony to think that one should devote oneself to prayer alone and not touch any work at all. Do not allow the orthodox to assemble with the so-called Meletians, so that they do not become sharers in their apostasy. If the Meletians repent and come over to the orthodox, let them be received. But let no one be indifferent, and let no one have communion with them while they do not repent, so that, as I said, they do not become sharers in their false belief. Let your Piety arrange for these things to be read out in those monasteries, to build up the people there, and let it instruct them to keep them. Then the orthodox will not grow weary as their conscience is undermined, and those who want to be fed in idleness will have no opening to seem to be good. I pray that you fare well in the Lord, beloved and most dear.

CHAPTER ONE. Those who are of sound mind, and who turn the keen [eye] of their understanding to discussions of the ineffable Godhead, see that it lies beyond everything that has come into being. It rises above even the sharpest mind and is wholly beyond anything the bodily imagination can picture, and, as the all-wise Paul says, it dwells in unapproachable light. But if the light around it is unapproachable, how could anyone behold it? For we see in a mirror and in a riddle, and we know in part. The Divine, then, is incorporeal, without quantity or magnitude, and does not have a circumscribed form. How could something whose nature is like this be thought of as made up of parts and members? If anyone granted that this were true, it could no longer be thought of as incorporeal. For whatever has a shape at all is surely also in quantity and in place, and whatever is thought of as being in a place is not beyond circumscription. These are properties of bodies, but they are wholly foreign to the incorporeal nature. So we must not think of God as having eyes or ears, or hands and feet, or wings, unless someone should perhaps choose to think of such things not as they exist in tangible, gross bodies but as in something subtle and immaterial, in keeping with the nature of God. For it is utterly simple-minded to want to imagine anything of the sort. God is spirit, and being spirit he knows all things; he watches over all things and surveys them, and nothing that exists escapes him. When divine Scripture mentions parts or members in speaking to us about him, we must understand that it addresses us in terms of what we know and of what we are by nature. Otherwise we could not grasp anything about God. The true cause and reason why the God-inspired Scripture speaks to us about God in bodily terms, then, is the poverty of our minds and tongues. What concerns him is wholly beyond words, and those who live in tangible, gross bodies could not understand what they need to know unless, in the manner …

To those who say that the soul was created [from] the breath, as the body was from hands [?]; to those who suppose that that breath became the soul for man; and to others who say that that breath gave the created man life-giving power as a whole, that the mind is this breath and is distinct from the soul, and that this is what "according to the image" means, so that man is made up of these three, body, soul and mind, each distinct within the union [?]; and on whether this breath belongs to the essence of God or is foreign to it. Questions as subtle and untrodden as these do not call for a dogmatic pronouncement [?], but rather for testing by conjecture, taking care not to let the argument slip into what is unfitting, that is, to be carried beyond what is reasonable. For it is written, "If you inquire, inquire, and dwell with me." But how could anyone explain clearly what the sacred Scripture has not stated clearly? What I mean is this. It is written at the [beginning] of the account of the world's creation: "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth." The sacred Scripture said that he made them, and we accept this in faith as true. But it is not without harm to inquire curiously how, or from what, or in what way heaven and earth and the rest of the creatures were brought into existence, for we should not plunge our minds into things too deep for us. So whatever divine Scripture does not state clearly should remain hidden and be passed over in silence. But if we must also make a conjecture, with reasoning aimed at what is correct, we say this: the Creator of all fashioned man from the earth, that is, the body; and having given it life with a living, intelligent soul, in the way he knows, he naturally implanted in it a longing for every good thing and a knowledge of it. I think this is what is meant by the words of the blessed evangelist John: "He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world." For the living creature is born with a natural aptitude for the good. The all-wise Paul teaches this clearly when he writes, "For we are his …"

… a partaker of the Holy [Spirit], so that it might bear the marks of the divine nature in itself more brightly, he breathed into it the breath of life. This is the Spirit that is supplied through the Son to rational creation and shapes it into the highest form, that is, the divine. The Spirit breathed into man did not become a soul for him, nor indeed a mind, as some think, and this can be seen from the following. First, the one who breathed is understood to be God, and what was breathed out from him must surely be understood as belonging to him, that is, to his essence. Next, how could the Spirit from God have been changed into the nature of a soul, or have become a mind? For it is impossible for the Spirit to undergo change. But even if someone were to grant that it did, and that it became soul or mind by a change (which is one of the impossible things), one can see the following at once. If the divine Spirit had become a soul for man, the soul and the mind would have remained incapable of sin. But if the Spirit from God was changed into a soul and then fell into sins, we bring a double charge against it: first, that it underwent a change into what it was not; and second, that we say it became capable of sin. So the living creature was given a soul by the ineffable power of God, and it came to be in his likeness, in that it is by nature good and just and capable of every virtue. It was sanctified by being made a partaker of the divine Spirit, and this it also lost through sin. For God says somewhere, "My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh," that is, because they think only of the things of the flesh. But when God the Father was pleased to sum up all things in Christ, that is, to bring them back to their original state, he restored to us the Holy Spirit that had flown away and departed from us, and breathed it on the holy apostles, saying, "Receive the Holy Spirit." For what came through Christ is a renewal of that ancient gift and of the breath once given to us. It reshapes us into the first sanctification and brings human nature back, with the holy apostles as the firstfruits, to the sanctification given to us at the beginning, in the first creation.

Likewise, on man being according to the image of God. They say that others too are asking how we should understand man to be according to the image of God, and that some then say, quite unintelligently, that the likeness to God is the image of the body, the visible form itself, and nothing else. So I thought it necessary to say that they have gone astray and that their minds have no love for contemplating the truth. For although the Saviour clearly says, "God is spirit," they say that the divine nature is bodily, and has such a shape as …

…as we are. Then he too would be a body, and would no longer be conceived of as spirit, for forms certainly belong to bodies. But since God is spirit, he is surely without form, and beyond every outline, shape and limit. We have been formed after him first, and in the most proper sense, so far as this can be understood, by virtue and sanctification. For the Divine is holy, and is the origin, source and beginning of all virtue. That it is more fitting to understand the statement that man was made in the image of God in this way, the all-wise Paul will also teach when he says to those in Galatia: "My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you." For Christ is formed in us through the sanctification that comes through the Spirit, through the calling in faith in him. But in those who transgress the faith his features do not shine out soundly. That is why they need another spiritual labor and a spiritual rebirth, so that, as the Holy Spirit makes the divine image flash forth in them through sanctification, they may once again be re-formed into Christ. It is not implausible to say that man's likeness to God also lies in his rule, for he has been given rule over all things on earth. This is the second sense of the likeness to God. But if being fashioned or made in the image of the Creator lay in the nature and appearance of the human body, how could anyone lose it? For we have lost nothing of what belongs to our essential being. But since sanctification and righteousness form us after God, we say that those who no longer lived according to virtue and in sanctification have cast off that so venerable and exceptional beauty. That is why it is recovered through sanctification and virtue and a life of godliness. And if some, out of great frivolity, suppose that the divine nature has human shape, how could the Savior say to the Jews about God the Father: "Truly, truly I say to you, you have never heard his voice or seen his form"? For if he had human shape, as I said, how is it that not only the Jews but all people have not seen his form?

When we interpreted "in the image of God" as applied to man, we did not say that the shape of the body was modeled on him. For the Divine is incorporeal, immaterial and intangible, beyond quantity and limit, form and shape. In applying the divine image to man, we said that he was made after the likeness of

the Creator himself in the quality of his character and conduct, and in the spiritual form displayed [?] through the beauty of the virtues. For the Divine is present in every good thing, and is itself the source, root and origin of all virtue, and from there good things come to us as well. If, then, we are formed after God by the form that the virtues produce, and this is also found in the holy angels, and incomparably more than in us, it is not hard to see that every rational creature is formed after God through sanctification and righteousness and every virtue. For if the divine, heavenly beauty is fitting for us who live on earth, how much more for the rational powers above, on whom God rests? This is why the divine Scriptures call heaven his throne [?].

Against those who say that we received "in the image" as soon as we were created, but did not receive "in the likeness" at all, since it is reserved for us in the age to come. For this reason, they say, it is written: "When Christ appears, we shall be like him." And again it is said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness"; yet after the creation of man it says: "God made man; in his own image he made him," passing over "in the likeness" in silence, to show that we have not yet received it but that it is reserved for us in that blessed life. If they claim that "in the image" and "in the likeness" are different things, let them explain the difference. For our position is that "in the image" means nothing other than "in the likeness," and likewise "in the likeness" means nothing other than "in the image." We received the likeness to God in our original making, and we are an image of God. For, as I said, the constitution of man, or rather his nature, is capable of receiving goodness, righteousness and sanctification, and has the desire for them implanted in it by God. This can be seen from the following: the human mind swerved, and not from evil toward good but from good toward evil. So we must first take as a premise the very thing we abandoned when we turned away. That a desire and eagerness for every good, and a knowledge of it, were sown in the human soul from its original making, the all-wise Paul will make clear when he says: "For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they are a law to themselves even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness." If even the Gentiles outside the law naturally know the law, that is, the lawgiver's purpose, it will be clear to everyone that human nature was righteous and good in the beginning, and was brought into being by God for this, bearing his form and the image of his goodness. For the first period of human life was holy; but when sin crept in, the features of our likeness to God no longer stayed bright in us. But since

It is pointless to say that this is reserved for us in the age to come. For when God said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," who would dare to say that man was made in the image but not also in the likeness? We shall be like Christ in incorruptibility, in becoming stronger than death, and indeed in the glory that he will grant us. For the divine Paul writes again: "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, who is our life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory." And again he says: "who will transform our lowly body so that it is conformed to his glorious body." Even now we are not without his likeness, if it is true that he is formed in us through the Holy Spirit. For again Paul writes to the Galatians: "My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you." When we keep ourselves faithful and holy, then Christ is seen being formed in us, making his own features flash out in our minds.

Against those who say that we are not the image of God but the image of the image. Their argument runs: the Son, who is also the Word of God the Father, is his image, but man is an image not of the archetype but of the image, that is, of the Son, so that we are an image of an image. For it is not said, they claim, that God made man "as his image" but "according to the image," so that man would be according to the image of God the Father, that is, an image of the Son, which makes him an image of an image. Our answer: the divine and consubstantial Trinity is beyond every form and every bodily picture. We must believe that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and that whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father. And the Son is also seen in the consubstantial Spirit, for it is written: "Now the Lord is the Spirit." Where there is complete identity of substance, there can surely be no difference at all. Whatever you conceive the Father to be, that the Son is too, except only

for being Father; and whatever you take the Son to be, that the Spirit is too, except for being Son. For each of those named subsists in his own distinct way, and truly is what he is said to be. But the likeness within the holy Trinity holds without variation in every respect. So even if man was made according to the image of the Son, he is in this way also according to the image of God. For the features of the whole holy Trinity shine in him, since the Godhead by nature in Father, Son and Holy Spirit is one. Thus Moses, the God-inspired, writes: "And God said, Let us make man in our image and likeness." The word "our" does not indicate a single person, because the fullness of the divine and ineffable nature exists in three hypostases. It is pointless, then, to fuss over subtleties and argue that we are images not of God himself, nor of the archetype, but of God's image. It is enough to believe in simplicity that we were made according to the divine image, having received by nature a form patterned on God. And if one may add something not implausible, it was fitting that we, who were to be called sons of God, should be made according to the image of the Son in particular, so that the mark of sonship might shine in us as well.

Against those who say that in the future state the soul, being rational and therefore not lacking knowledge, will make progress; and that if it is capable of progress, it must also be capable of decline, passion and corruption, and therefore of death and renewed life. Those who think this way seem not to know the grace that will be given to human nature after its return to life from the dead. For if this corruptible body must put on incorruption and strip off corruption, then along with corruption we shall clearly also cast off the passions that arise from it, namely all fleshly desire. From then on we shall be transferred into a holy and spiritual life, as Christ, the Savior of us all, grants us steadfastness in these things. For if now, having only the pledge of the Spirit, we live holy lives, what shall we be when we have received it in full? And where there is the fullness of the Spirit, there is surely also security of mind and firmness of heart, a heart that looks to the good and to the pure vision of God. We shall therefore be better than we are now, having put off corruption and having a spiritual body, that is, looking only to the things of the spirit. And at that time there will be no wavering to drag us down into wickedness, since the Creator will hold us fast to his [will] through the Holy Spirit, just as he does the holy angels. Christ declared something of this kind when he said: "In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven."

…all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive." So the universal and most general penalty, which came through the transgression in Adam, is corruption and death; likewise the redemption of all, also most general, has been accomplished in Christ. For in him human nature put off the death that had been cast upon it when the first man became corruptible. But the father of each of us, even if he was sanctified through the Holy Spirit and received forgiveness of his offenses, will not pass the gift on to us as well. For there is one who sanctifies and justifies all and restores them to incorruption, our Lord Jesus Christ, and through him the gift comes to all equally. Forgiveness of sin is one thing, and release from death is another. Each person gains forgiveness of his own offenses in Christ through the Holy Spirit, but all of us together are freed from the penalty imposed on us in the beginning, I mean death, which spread to all after the likeness of the first man, who fell into death. This is why the all-wise Paul says that death reigned from Adam to Moses even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam's transgression: until the law, the penalty of death held sway. But once Christ had shone forth, righteousness came in, justifying

Whether the resurrection that the prophet Ezekiel saw has already taken place, when bone came to bone and joint to joint, along with flesh, skin, hair and spirit, and the rising of a great multitude was seen; or whether the divine Scripture showed us, in a vision, an image of the universal resurrection that is still to come. [?] Some events are so great, and so far beyond belief in the wonder they arouse, that they are viewed with suspicion and even disbelieved by some. So the prophets were sometimes taught such things not by announcement alone, with the Holy Spirit making the knowledge of each flash out to them, but also saw them in actual events, so that they would believe first themselves and then set them out for others. So the God of all, who had promised to bring back to Jerusalem even those who had already died in Babylon (surely not the earthly Jerusalem at all, but the one above, which is understood to be in the heavens), clearly showed the prophet the resurrection and the way it will take place in its time. The divine David also foretold this, speaking about us, that is, about every human being: "When you turn away your face, they will be dismayed, and they return to their dust. You will send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth." For having offended in Adam through the transgression, we were turned away from God, and for this reason we returned to our own dust, having come under the curse. For the Creator said: "Earth you are, and to earth you shall return." But in the last times of the age, by the power of the life-giving Spirit, God the Father will raise all the dead in Christ. That the resurrection of the dead has not yet happened but will come in its time, the all-wise Paul will confirm when he writes that "Hymenaeus and Alexander have suffered shipwreck in the faith, saying that the resurrection has already taken place." If whoever says this suffers shipwreck in the faith, it is clear that the blessed prophet Ezekiel saw the power of the resurrection, for our benefit, as in a prophetic vision.

Against those who ask whether Christ, by coming in the flesh, added anything to human nature, and in what sense man is in the image of God. Who would not dare to say that Christ, by his coming, became the source of every good thing for human nature? Or who will deny it and say that his being sent into this world did us no good? In the beginning man was made in God's image, and his nature was well suited to taking up every good thing and to

achieving virtue. "For he created us for good works," as the all-wise Paul writes. But sin obliterated the beauty of the godlike image, and Satan made the bright face of humanity filthy. But the Renewer appeared, restoring what had been wronged to its original state and refashioning us again into his own image, so that the features of his divine nature shine in us through sanctification, righteousness and a good and virtuous life. For he is the door and the way through which we have been able to reach every one of the best things and make our paths straight, so that in us who are in Christ the beauty of the best of images shines out, if we prove ourselves by our very deeds. In the first-formed man there was every aptitude, carrying the capacity to take up virtue, but not yet, by any means, its actual exercise. That is why Christ himself said about us, that is, about his own sheep: "I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly." For what was in Adam in the beginning, namely sanctification, has been restored to human nature. And by "abundantly," I think, he means actually practising [?] virtue and being made radiant through good deeds themselves.

That we can restrain [?] the pleasures of the flesh, but cannot cut them out entirely. To some the all-wise Paul seems to say things that are difficult, or hard to understand, in the words of the holy apostles. But there can be no doubt that these things are full of the wisdom from above, for Christ speaks in him. He says, then: "I delight in the law of God in my inner self, but I see another law in my members, waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin." And again: "Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord." When the mind looks to self-control out of the fear of God, the movement of the flesh campaigns against it, opposes its impulses toward purity, and fights back fiercely. But those who keep a fitting sobriety and worship God rebuke the movement of the flesh and blunt the goad of sin by ascetic discipline and toil, and by using other suitable means. So it is not possible to uproot the flesh's innate desire; but by sobriety, as I said, it is possible to keep it from growing bold against the mind. This is all the more so because the only-begotten Word of God has become man and no longer allows the law of sin in our members, savage as it is, to run riot against us. The most excellent Paul will teach this clearly when he writes: "For what the law could not do, weakened as it was

by the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and to deal with sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the just requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit." We shall therefore prevail over our innate impulses, though not completely or entirely, for that is reserved for the all-blessed life we expect in the age to come. But we can act courageously and rebuke the impulses of the flesh, with God working alongside us and supplying us with power from on high. In the negligent, desire is stronger and, as it were, rules over their hearts; but in those who have the fear of God it is feeble, easily rebuked and driven out of the mind. For it is written that the law of the Lord is pure, that is, it makes pure.

That the Eucharist must be celebrated only in the catholic churches. The gift, that is, the offering that we perform as a mystery, must be offered only in the holy churches of the orthodox and nowhere else; those who do otherwise plainly break the law. This can be seen from the sacred Scriptures. The law commanded that the lamb be sacrificed on the day, that is, the feast, of Passover, and it was a type of Christ. "But it shall be eaten in one house," it says, "and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside." So those who do not celebrate in the one catholic house of Christ, that is, the Church, carry the gift outside. [?] Something similar is signified by another law, for it is also written: "And whoever sacrifices a calf or a sheep in the camp and does not bring it to the door of the tent, that soul shall be utterly destroyed from among its people." So those who sacrifice outside the tent can be none other than the heretics, and destruction hangs over those who dare to do this. We therefore believe that the offerings made in the churches are consecrated, blessed and perfected by Christ.

That we must not inquire into God's [?] … (7) "The law of the Lord is pure," etc.: so called from its effect, as Homer calls sheep "sturdy," that is, making strong [?] … for the law [commanded] the lamb to be sacrificed [?] … he concludes thus: "If we should be asked whether all things to God [?]

…power, which is great and admirable, [?] that what is done is not out of keeping with the divine glory. For it does not follow that, because he can do all things, he should be seen to work absurdities. We recognize that it is absurd to ask: Can God make himself not to be God? Can he make himself capable of sin? Can he make himself not to be good, or life, or just? Such absurd questions must therefore be refused with all our strength. Why can God never make a woman who has committed fornication not to have been a harlot? Because falsehood cannot make truth. This is not a charge of weakness. It shows a nature that will not allow itself to undergo anything unfitting to it, and falsehood is utterly foreign to it. It would be a falsehood to make the woman who fornicated never to have fornicated. As I said, such foolish and absurd questions should not even be entertained in the first place.

Against those who say that the Son did not know the last day; against the Agnoetae. They say that others, hearing Christ say, "About that day or hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father alone," most foolishly claim that the Word, who came forth from the substance of God the Father, truly does not know either the hour or that day. This would rank him with the angels, so that he would in no way differ from the things made through him. But then how can the thing made and its Maker be of equal rank and nature? And how is the distance between them not infinite? For the one is beyond all things, the other is among all things. If they think that Christ was truly ignorant of anything insofar as he is understood to be God, they have gone wide of the mark. They are running against rocks and raising the horn against his glory. If things were as they say, it would turn out that he is no longer consubstantial with God the Father. For if the Father knows and the Son does not know, how will the Son be equal to him, that is, consubstantial? The one who does not know must certainly be less than the one who knows. And what is still more unreasonable, the Son has been called the Counsel of God the Father. Paul said of him, "Who became for us wisdom from God"; and again, "In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." And the inspired David sings to the Father and God in heaven, "Lord, in your counsel you have guided me," calling the Son who was born from him his counsel. How, then, is it not ridiculous to think that anything in the Father is unknown to — [?] possible, let us answer, the things fitting to him, and every [?] useless inquiry. For he can do all things,

his wisdom and his counsel? And how can he who knows the Father [?] be ignorant of the day of the consummation? Which is the greater knowledge: to know what the Father is, or to know the last day? It is also written, "The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God." Since the Spirit, who knows the depths of God and all that is in him, is also the Spirit of the Son himself, how can the Son not know what is in his own Father? Many considerations thus drive their ignorant and counterfeit argument into absurdity. So we must turn to the economy and say that, together with humanity, the only-begotten Word of God also took on all its properties, except sin alone. Ignorance of things to come may reasonably belong to the measures of humanity. Therefore, insofar as he is understood to be God, he knows all that the Father knows. But insofar as the same one is man, he does not refuse even to seem ignorant, because this befits humanity. He is the life and power of all, yet he took bodily food without scorning the measure of his self-emptying, and Scripture records that he slept and grew weary. In the same way, though he knew all things, [he was not ashamed to assign to himself] the ignorance befitting the incarnation, that is, the enfleshment, of the Only-begotten. [?] speaking of the divine incarnation [?] "incarnate without seed" [?] of the first-formed had already come about, [?] of the Lord's [?] using the servile [nature] for the ineffable economy [?]. He calls it "economy" in Letter 456: the incarnate Manifestation of the Son of God that took place on behalf of human sins [?], that is, saving [?]. He makes him say: "For the salvation of sinners I will carry out that economy." [?] the incarnate economy joining [?] from us, that is, perfect; [?] to infants rather, he accepted [?] by way of economy for their sake, so that they might become perfect. That is, the Law [?] the Lord's economy. He states this opinion as follows: "God, through Isaiah, reproaches those who take no care to live the best life but find fault with his economies. He says, 'They desire to know my ways, like a people that has done righteousness and has not forsaken the judgment of its God.' [?] those who [?] his ways, that is, his economies, would be utterly reckless; [?] go no further [?] in daring, who stir up talk about God himself with a defiled tongue, and especially when [?] the economy of God, [?] and counsels

[the ignorance proper to] humanity he is not ashamed to assign to himself. For everything belonging to humanity became his, except sin alone. The disciples wanted to learn things beyond their reach, so for their benefit he pleads that he does not know, insofar as he is man. He says that not even the holy angels in heaven know, so that the disciples would not be grieved as though they had not been trusted with the

Chapter 15. How we should understand "The Word became flesh." I learn that some claim to ask what "The Word became flesh" might mean, or in what way it is to be understood. So again we must say this: the divinely inspired Scripture sometimes names the human being by the flesh alone. Thus in the prophets God promised to pour out his Spirit on all flesh. And again it is said, "All flesh shall see the salvation of God." Surely we do not say that the divine Spirit is poured out on the flesh alone, or that the flesh alone has seen the salvation that comes through Christ. Rather, the Spirit was poured out on human beings, and it is they who have seen salvation. So when the evangelist says, "And the Word became flesh," he does not teach that the Word of God was changed into flesh (for he is unchangeable, as coming from an unchangeable Father). He teaches that the Word made his own a flesh animated by a rational soul and came forth wondrously as a man from the holy Virgin. He was not first a man who was afterwards deified. Being God by nature, he became man.

Against those who [?] that each has [already received] a worthy recompense. [Why] the Saviour did not say "a certain poor man" but "Lazarus": so that by the name [?] and truth [?] the story had actually taken place. The divine Scripture says that the judgment will come after the resurrection from the dead. And there will be no resurrection until Christ comes to us again from heaven in the glory of the Father with the holy angels. [?] the all-wise Paul also says, "The [?] united to him, [?] his own [?] flesh [?] rational, he says. In others [?] animated with a human rational [soul]. [?]

Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead in Christ will be raised incorruptible." The Judge of all has not yet come down from heaven, so the resurrection of the dead has not yet taken place either. How, then, is it not implausible to think that some have already been repaid for their evil or good deeds? The words of Christ about the rich man and Lazarus are therefore an elegantly composed parable. According to the tradition of the Hebrews, there was at that time in Jerusalem a man named Lazarus, suffering from extreme poverty and sickness. The Lord mentioned him, taking him as an example to make his teaching clearer. Christ, the Saviour of all, has not yet come down from heaven, so there has been no resurrection, and no one has yet received the recompense for their deeds. Instead the parable depicts, as in an image, a rich man who lived in luxury and had no pity, and a poor man in sickness. It does this so that those who have wealth on earth may know what awaits them. Unless they choose to be kind, generous and ready to share, and decide to help the poor in their needs, they will fall into a terrible and inescapable punishment.

Against those who say: How did the demons, being incorporeal, have intercourse with women? Since, he says, some are asking how the wicked demons, being incorporeal, had intercourse with women, and how the women bore the giants from them, we must speak briefly on this too. We will not stretch ourselves out in lengthy narratives, but set out the sense of the matter as in summary. They say, then, that in the earliest times or ages there was a division between those descended from Cain and those descended from Enos. Because of his very great righteousness, Enos was called "god" by the people of that time. "For he hoped," it says, "to call on the name of the Lord his God." Those descended from Enos were devoted to righteousness and every good work, following their father's ways. Those descended from Cain were insolent and accursed, and readily practised every kind of wickedness, for their father was like that too. As long as the two races were kept apart from one another, those descended from Enos continued to excel in the best way of life. But, it says, the sons of the one called god, that is, of Enos, saw the daughters of Cain (whom Scripture also called the daughters of men). Then they were corrupted [?] [?] by the name of God [?]

with them. They gave in to shameful lusts and turned to the ways of those people. God was angered, and he caused the women they had chosen to bear misshapen monsters. These were also called giants because of their hideous and harsh manners and their savage insolence. Indeed, the four translators who came after the Seventy did not write "The sons of God, seeing the daughters of men" when they rendered this passage. Some wrote "The sons of the rulers," and others "The sons of the mighty." It is foolish to think that incorporeal demons can perform the acts of bodies and do what is contrary to their own nature. Nothing that exists can do what is contrary to its nature. Each thing remains as it was made, in the order fixed by [?]. For he is the Creator and Lord of all, by whose nod each existing thing is what it is. In this connection one should also know that some copies read, "The angels of God, seeing the daughters of men." But this is a gloss inserted from outside. The true reading is "The sons of God, seeing the daughters of men."

Chapter [?]. Against those who say that when the Son became man and was on earth, he was with the Father according to the dignity of the Godhead, but no longer according to hypostasis. I learn that some people talk rashly and thoughtlessly, as they usually do, even about matters so great and so necessary. They say something like this: when the only-begotten Son of God dwelt on earth and lived among men, he was with the Father according to the dignity of the Godhead and substance, since he is consubstantial with him, but according to the principle of hypostasis, no longer. For, as they say, the whole filial hypostasis had emptied itself out of the heavens and out of the Father's very bosom, because one hypostasis must not be joined to another, not even when they exist in one substance. I was amazed at the ignorant rashness of those who think this, and I thought it necessary to say the following. In their view the substance of God has been reduced to a quantity. They make it comprehensible and bounded, no longer unlimited or incomprehensible, but now contained in places and enclosed by dimensions. But these things belong to the definition of bodies. Therefore God would also be a body, and surely one with a form, not without a body; for such properties go with bodies. How, then, does the Saviour say, "God is spirit"? He says that God is spirit in order to lead our thought of that transcendent and ineffable nature beyond bodily imaginings. Could one not justly say to those who have prattled such things, or dare to think them, "Sodom has been justified by you"? For the wise among the Greeks hold a more pious opinion of the Divine. They affirm that it is incorporeal and formless,

without quantity, without parts and without shape, present everywhere and absent from nothing. And how did they fail to notice this? Suppose the Son, who is consubstantial with the Father, emptied heaven of his presence when he became man and lived among those on earth. Then it follows that the earth was empty of the Father's hypostasis, since the Father did not himself become man or live among men, but — to put it in terms of their folly — remained in the heavens. How, then, did the Saviour say, "The Father who dwells in me does the works himself"? And how does he say through the prophet, "Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord"; and again, "I am a God near at hand, says the Lord, and not a God far off"? For Christ, who was begotten of the Father by nature, has all things near, filling all things together with the Father. Indeed the prophet David says, "Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?" It is not possible, it is simply not possible, ever to find heaven or earth empty of the ineffable Godhead. As I said, the divine and consubstantial Trinity fills all things. We remember too that the Saviour and Lord of all said to the holy apostles, "It is to your advantage that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you." When he had gone, he kept his promise and sent us the Paraclete from heaven, that is, the Spirit, who is consubstantial with the Father and the Son. So when the Paraclete came down to earth to sanctify us, was the Spirit no longer in the heavens? Or should one say that, having sanctified us, the Spirit went back up to heaven and is not with us? Yet it is written that the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world. Christ himself also said, when he was about to ascend to the Father, "Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the end of the age." But if he is with us, then by their reasoning the heavens are surely empty even now of the "filial hypostasis," as they call it. He has left the Father's bosom and lives instead with those on earth. This is the frigid nonsense they talk, as I said. Who could tolerate their recklessness? Or who among the more sensible would not shed abundant tears over them? They are ignorant of the sacred and divine Scriptures. They spew out whatever comes into their minds without examining it, and fall away from the correct doctrines of the Church. What did the Son say to Philip when Philip spoke to him about the Father? "Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me?" So it is impossible for the one ever to be without the other. Wherever the Father is understood to be (and he is everywhere), there surely the Son is too; and wherever the Son is, there the Father is as well. For if the Son is the radiance of the Father, and his Word, wisdom and power, how could the Fa-

-ther ever be conceived of without Word, power and wisdom? And how could the wisdom of God, his Word and power ever be conceived of without the Father? How could his exact image ever fail to exist in him? And how could the image exist without the Father? But, they say, it is not [?], because one hypostasis must not be joined to another, not even when they exist in one substance. Perhaps they bring forward our own human conditions as proof of their nonsense. Should they not have understood that the properties and distinctive features of the divine nature are not governed by what applies to us? They have their own principles. They are received by faith and do not tolerate overly curious reasoning. For the nature of the ineffable Godhead is one, in three distinct hypostases. It lies beyond our categories and does not follow the customs of created things. This can be seen in many ways. We are fathers of our own children by emanation and division, for what is begotten departs completely into a separate otherness. But we do not say that the Son was begotten of God the Father in this way. He shone forth from the Father's substance and beamed out like light, yet he did not come to be outside him. He is both from him and in him. Again, among us fathers are older than their own children, but this is not at all true of God. The Son always coexists with the Father, and his existence is without beginning, like that of his own Begetter, so that the Father may always be seen to be Father; for there was never a time when this was not so. The divine Offspring, who is above the world, is therefore the same in nature as the Father. He differs only by the otherness that belongs to sonship: he is not father, just as the Father is not son. Therefore, as I said, the supreme substance fills all things, because it is above creation, mind and reason. So let no one babble, speaking things from their own heart and not from the mouth of the Lord, as it is written. Otherwise, by corrupting the truth, they will bring down on their own souls the punishment that befits those who habitually do this.

Against those who say that when the Only-begotten became man he left the heavens empty of his own Godhead. Some, as I have learned, spread about incredible little phrases full of the utmost absurdity. They speak things from their own heart and not from the mouth of the Lord, as it is written. For where the beauty of the truth does not shine through, the father of lies is surely there, pouring out the murderous poison of the malice within him. I learn, then, that some people, out of very great folly, hold and say that the only-begotten Word of God left the heavens empty of his own Godhead when he became man and lived in the flesh among those on earth. But this is nothing other than saying that he can be measured by quantity, that his nature can be circumscribed, and that he remains in a place

just as bodies do, that is, the other created things. Perhaps they did not know that the Divine is incorporeal, without shape and without parts. It cannot be measured by quantity or circumscribed by place. It fills all things and is in all things, while by its own nature it cannot be contained. For it is written, "Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I go up into heaven, you are there; if I go down into Hades, you are present. If I take up my wings at dawn and settle at the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me." So they should not spew out rash words out of ignorance. They should consider what kind of nature God's divine, surpassingly great and ineffable nature is, how great it is, and in what ways it excels. For how [variant: when] did God the Word ever cease to be with the Father, or to remain in him? If it were possible for the radiance to fall away from the light and be separated from it, it would be reasonable to think that the Son might not be with the Father. Did they not realize that the sun, which had a beginning, behaves otherwise? It is a creature, brought into being through the Word himself. It travels the path above that was appointed to it, yet it sends its light down in every direction and fills all things with the brightness that pours out from it, while still holding that brightness within itself. When, then, was the radiance of his glory not in the Father? When was his exact image separated from his hypostasis? If the Father fills all things, does the Son not have this by nature too — I mean filling all things, being everywhere, and being absent from nothing? If not, then he is of a different nature from the Father. So those who dare to say these things about him fall into the erroneous opinion of the Arians. If they truly believe that the Son is God and was born by nature from God the Father, why do they not grant him what befits the divine nature? If they dress him up with the name of God but deprive him of the dignities of the Godhead, they fail to see that they are bringing the Maker down among the creatures and ranking the Creator and Lord of all among the things that were made. So while he was seen on earth as a man according to the flesh, even then the heavens were full of his Godhead. For the Word, being God, fills all things.

Against those who say that the Word alone works the divine signs, and that his holy flesh has no part in this. But those who say that the flesh must not be made to share — When, then, was the radiance not in the Father? [?] The divine Paul, as though inspired, went beyond all earthly examples and defined the Son as the "radiance of glory" and the "exact image of the Father's hypostasis." [?] by the first [example] [he showed] that the Son is coeternal, and by the second example that the
[Son], begotten of the Father before every age and time, [is] God, and his only-begotten and subsistent Word; he calls [?]

[?] …to the divinity of the Only-begotten, nor the divinity to the flesh in the miracles; or again, that it was not a man who raised Lazarus from the tomb by calling him, but God the Word; and that it was not God who grew weary on the journey, but the man who was assumed, and that this man hungered and thirsted and was crucified and died — such people, we say, have entirely missed the truth and failed to understand the mystery of the economy in the flesh. For we do not say that there are two Sons, nor two Christs, but one Christ and Son: begotten as God from God the Father before every age and time, his only-begotten and subsistent Word, and in the last times of the age the same one, according to the flesh, born of a woman. So let them not split him apart as though he had two souls [?], nor bring two Sons in upon us, but let them confess one and the same, God the Word made man, and that everything is his, both the sayings and the actions. For since the same one was at once God and man, he speaks both as befits God and as a man, and he likewise performs both human acts and acts befitting God. When, then, they do not confess one Son and Christ and Lord, they will be found [?] ignorantly dividing him and separating him into two, so that one Son is understood individually and apart, the Word from God the Father [?], and another Son again individually and apart, the man who, as they put it, was assumed. We do not speak this way, nor do we believe this way. We believe that God the Word became flesh without casting off his being God. He remained what he was, unchangeably and unalterably, and partook of flesh and blood according to the Scriptures; and the flesh united to him and made his own, we say, was endowed with a soul [?].

Against those who say that he was not taken up with the flesh united to him. [?] Against those who say that the Lord's body has been blended with the Holy Trinity. That he was taken up together with the flesh united to him, how could anyone doubt? The one raised from the dead — clearly himself, insofar as he appeared and is understood as man — the Father has seated at the right hand of the throne of majesty on high, far above every rule and authority and power and dominion and every name that is named. And in this way he will come at the appointed time. For this the voice of the holy angels will be enough, who cried out openly to those watching him ascend after his return from the dead to life: "This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven." If, then, those who witnessed his ascension saw the Word stripped of flesh, let some suppose that he will come that way. But if he fully assured the holy apostles by showing them his tangible body, and was taken up in that way, then that is how he will come again, and the word of the holy apostles about him will not prove false.

But let no one wrongly imagine or suspect that the body united to the Word has been blended with the nature of the Holy Trinity. For it is impossible that that ineffable and supernatural essence, conceived as beyond all mind and reason, could receive any addition, least of all from an external and different nature. It is all-perfect in what belongs to it, and admits no diminution, because it is always unchangeable and unalterable; nor, as I said, could it need any addition. Those, then, who out of great ignorance say that the body has passed into the nature of the Holy Trinity by blending or union of essence are talking idle nonsense. That is not our position; we hold the right belief about Christ, the Savior of us all. For we say that the only-begotten Word himself, God [from God], became man, not changing his own nature into flesh, but taking flesh from the holy Virgin, and that he will come again with it in the glory of the [Father?] with the holy [angels?] [?].

That God the Word works the divine signs through his own flesh. We say that the only-begotten Word of God became man, not so that he might cast off being God, nor so that he might be thought of as the bare Word, but rather that he became man and made his own the body from the Virgin and Theotokos. So whoever names Christ means neither the bare Word nor an ordinary man, or one of us, but, as I said, the Word from God the Father made man and anointed for his mission. For it was not a man who was deified by being united to the Word, as some say. Rather the Word himself took flesh and became man, and even so remained God. When, therefore, he works the divine signs, do not separate the Word from God from his holy flesh and attach the power for the sign being performed to him alone (15). Rather, understand piously that the only-begotten Word of God, having become man, often acted through his own flesh, as having it as his own, not by confusion or mingling. Just as one may understand of a man who is a carpenter, say, or a craftsman, or a smith, that the soul does the work by means of its own body — and no one would say that the work belongs to the soul alone, even though it is the soul that moves the body to work, but to both together — so understand it in the case of Christ too. Before the incarnation the Word, still bare and by himself, performs the works befitting God; but having become man, he acted also through his flesh, as I said. So he touched the blind; so he raised the widow's son, stretching out his hand and touching the bier; so, spitting and making clay, he anointed the eyes of the man blind from birth. But if… (15) "Attach the power for the divine sign being performed to him alone." In this [?]

…and lived spiritually, consider again that, in raising our condition to a spiritual way of life, he himself began the task in a human way, so that human nature might have a road and a starting point for being able to live no longer in a fleshly and pleasure-loving way, but rather in a holy and spiritual one. For he has become for us the beginning of every good. And for this reason he appeared as a man: so that, having freed our nature from the weakness that came in Adam, he might show it to be spiritual, in himself first of all.

Utterly senseless are those who have supposed, I do not know how, that Christ himself could sin, because by the economy he came to be in our form, took the form of a servant, and lived among people on earth. If he had departed from being what he was, or had passed over from being God to being only what we are, let them look in him for the faults of human weakness. But if he bore human nature precisely so that he might show in himself, as most powerful and stronger than sin, the nature that had grown weak in Adam, why do they busy themselves in vain over what they cannot find? And how have they forgotten him saying, "The ruler of the world is coming, and he has nothing in me"? The inventor of sin accuses all flesh, but the prying of his malice achieved nothing in Christ, for nothing at all was found in him. Indeed, he said to the Jews, "Which of you convicts me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?" Just as in Adam we were condemned through disobedience and the transgression of the commandment, so in Christ we have been justified through his utter sinlessness and his obedience, complete and blameless in every respect; and in this human nature has gained its boast. The curse, then, has been stopped, the mouth [?] of sin has been shut, and with it the power of death has been brought to nothing, withering away as if together with its own root. For if sin became for us the cause of all evils, the justification in Christ, which enters through obedience and is entirely without fault, will be the undoing of what befell us. So even if he bore Adam, as they say, he was not like that earthly man from the earth, but heavenly, incomparably better than the earthly. In him one may see human nature crowned with the praises of sinlessness, as the divinely inspired Scripture bears witness to him: "He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth."

Why the Lord did not [become man] at the beginning, but [at the end] of the ages granted human life the manifestation of his Godhead [?]. Because, being about to mingle with human life for the destruction of evil, he necessarily waited [until] [?] the demons, with the devil who leads them, refusing to remain in their rank at all, but filled with every injustice and greed and never sated with insolence [?], had driven humanity to the extreme of the passions. Then indeed, then the King of all, the Word of the Father, hating the tyranny of the one and pitying the misfortunes of the other, put on human nature and took his stand on the battle line. So trophies were set up, some already standing, some being raised, and others still in hope [?]. The barbarous host of the demons [?] of their general bewailed their misfortunes, while human nature hastened back to freedom. That is why the Psalmist urged those who were set free to sing a new song, for with prophetic eyes he beheld what was to come. [?]

…for the salvation of humanity he truly became man. At this someone might be puzzled and ask: Why did the economy of the incarnation not take place in earlier times, so that from then on everyone might come to know the mystery of Christ? But we have heard the Lord saying in the Gospels, "Father, the hour has come" — that is, the fitting time, foreordained before the foundation of the world for the salvation of humanity. If this were not so, he would not have said, "The Son of Man goes as it has been determined." Who has ever been so bold as to contradict so openly what the Lord declares? This time appeared fitting and suited to the divine will both because the all-pure one who served the mystery of Christ was then brought into the world, and because at that time the disease of evil, which had fallen upon human nature from the beginning, had reached its peak (according to the divine Gregory of Nyssa). For if he had become man earlier, the disease, still hidden in the depths, would not have come under treatment [?], nor would the nations have heard themselves called as they were then. For when the illness is still raw, as a wise man said — that is, when it has run deep into the humors — it is not easily drawn out by the pull of remedies. So, as has been said, God came down to earth at the right time: "For when the fullness of time had come," says Paul, "God sent forth his Son." At the right time, then, he also undertakes the work of healing. God did not dwell among us openly, nor did he use his divine sovereignty to draw the nations to himself even against their will, since he did not wish to violate our free will in any way whatever. Had that been his way, he would perhaps have become man in earlier times and wrought our salvation by sheer authority. And do not tell me that everyone before Christ is therefore free of blame, since, had he become man earlier, those who ended their lives in unbelief would not have perished through ignorance. Say nothing of the kind. For those who, as John of Damascus says, lived a most ascetic life, even if they had unknowingly gone astray in matters of faith, and were of so docile and well-disposed a soul that, once they had seen and heard, they readily…

…[for] the evil rooted by the enemy to sprout up [fully] [?]. Then, as the Gospel says, he laid the axe to the root. For the best physicians, when a fever smoulders within the body and is gradually kindled by the causes of disease, give way to the illness until the sickness reaches its peak, giving the patient no help from food… [Bonaventura Vulcanius's notes: ?] …not only did they not prevail, but they were completely blinded, since the intelligible Sun, as we said, was flashing there. The great Gregory, distinguished in theology, pointed to this when he said: "Did the Lord, when he appeared, save everyone, or there too only those who did not live [in faith] yet were ready to believe?" [?] Do not doubt this, for you have, before all others, the chief apostle Peter saying about it: "He went and preached to the spirits in prison, who once disobeyed." Hence the great Cyril [?] also said: "Just as God lived with those on earth in the flesh, so too in Hades he preached to the souls, having as his own mind the soul united to him." [?] No less did the most divine Damascene treat this matter, saying: "Just as he preached peace to those on earth, and became the cause of salvation to those who believed and a reproof of unbelief to those who disobeyed, so also to those in Hades." Thus, ordering all things wisely, so that neither should the good lose their goodness through ignorance, nor should the wicked have any excuse, saying, "If we had known, we would have believed," he preaches in Hades too, as has been said, things like those he preached to the living [?], and from there draws out those who are fit to be drawn; and like some splendid champion he returns from there with them. For even though, rising from the dead, he granted that final resurrection to all in common, not all went up with him as he rose from Hades, but only those who believed, as Gregory the Theologian says. From this, then, it has been shown that he became man at the fitting time, and that no one perished through ignorance, since all, as we said, became hearers of the divine proclamation. This was the answer we gave to the difficulty. The emperor, full of all understanding, raised no further objection; rather, he greatly admired God for having arranged this in the ways he alone knows. [Notes: ?] "Having his own mind": here "mind" (phronēma) is phronēsis, that is, sōphrosynē [?]. Finally, "we shall bear the image of the earthly" (or, as [?], "of the heavenly") [?] "this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal put on immortality" [?].

…help. But when the evil has become stationary, they apply their skill, once the whole disease has shown itself. In the same way, in healing those sick in soul, he waited for the disease of evil, which had overpowered nature, to be fully uncovered, so that nothing hidden might remain untreated, since the physician treats only what has come to light. For this reason he did not bring the cure through his own appearing even in the time of Noah, when all flesh had been corrupted in injustice, because the shoot of Sodom's wickedness had not yet sprung up. Nor does the Lord appear at the time of Sodom's overthrow, because many of the remaining evils still lay hidden in human nature. For where was Pharaoh, who fought against God? Where was the unbending wickedness of the Egyptians? Yet not even then — I mean in the time of the Egyptians' evils — was it the right moment for the Corrector of the universe to mingle with human life. The lawlessness of the Israelites also had to be revealed. The arrogance of the Assyrian kingdom and of Nebuchadnezzar, still smouldering in life, had to come into the open. The murder of the holy ones had to shoot up like some evil, thorny shoot from the devil's wicked root. The madness of the Jews against the saints of God had to be exposed — of those who killed the prophets and stoned those who were sent, and finally committed the outrage against Zechariah between the temple and the altar. Add to the list of wicked shoots Herod's slaughter of the children as well. When, then, the whole power of evil had sprung up from the wicked root and had grown in manifold forms in the choices of each generation, evil running wild unrecognized, then, as Paul says to the Athenians, "God, having overlooked the times of ignorance," comes in the last days — when there was no one who understood, no one who sought God; when all had turned aside and together become worthless; when all things had been shut up under sin; when sin abounded; when the darkness of evil had grown to its utmost measure. Then grace appeared; then the ray of the true light dawned; then the Sun of righteousness appeared to those who sat in darkness and shadow; then he crushed the many heads of the dragon, stepping on them with his foot through human flesh, crushing them into the ground and trampling them underfoot. And let no one think that what happens in life now proves false the account by which we say the Lord shone upon life in the last times. The objector will perhaps say: "He who waited for the times when evil would be revealed, so that he might remove it once it had grown, should surely have destroyed it root and branch [?], so that no remnant of it was left in life. Yet now murders, thefts, adulteries and all the worst crimes are dared." But let whoever looks at this resolve the doubt by an example from familiar things. As one can see when serpents are killed, the coil is not crushed at once along with the head, but…

…[one part] is dead while the other is still animated by its own fury and has not lost its vital movement. So too the slayer of the dragon: when the beast had grown great, having increased along with each successive generation of humanity, he destroyed its head — that is, the power that invents evils, the one with many heads — and takes no account of the coil behind it, leaving the movement in the dead beast as an occasion of training for those who come after.

Which head it was that was crushed. The one that brought in death by its wicked counsel, the one that cast death-bearing venom into man by its bite [?]. He, then, who destroyed the power of death crushed the power in the serpent's head, as the Prophet says. But the remaining coil of the beast, entwined with human life, as long as humanity is caught up in evil motions [?], keeps roughening life with the scales of sin. In power, however, it is dead, since its head has already been made useless. When time has run its course and all that moves comes to rest at the expected consummation of this life, then the tail, the last part of the Enemy, is abolished — and this is death. Thus the complete destruction of the Beast, that is, of evil, will come about, when all are called back to life through the resurrection: the righteous moved to the inheritance above, and those held fast by their sins handed over to the fire of Gehenna. CHAPTER [?]. That human usage knows to call the unwedded "uncorrupted" [?] (17). That great Moses (18), when the fire was kindled in the bush and the bush was not consumed, "I will turn aside…" BONAVENTURA VULCANIUS'S NOTES. (17) "Human usage knows to call the unwedded 'uncorrupted.'" "Uncorrupted" is used elegantly [?]… "Do you wish to destroy the world? Raze its cities. Do you wish to destroy [?]? Destroy its houses utterly. Do you wish to destroy households? Take the wife away from her yoke-mate, breaking the lawful bonds of marriage. Cities and the world must needs perish, or else drive the defilers of the marriage bed out of the whole world." (18) "That great Moses" [?] this [?]

"I will see this great sight," he says. By "crossing over" he does not mean, I think, a movement from place to place, but the crossing over of time. What was then prefigured in the flame and the bush was clearly revealed in the mystery of the Virgin once the intervening time had passed. There the bush kindles the light and is not burned. In the same way the Virgin here gives birth to the light and is not corrupted. If the bush prefigures the God-bearing body of the Virgin, do not be ashamed of the riddle. Because all flesh has taken in sin, flesh is sin by the very fact that it is only flesh. And Scripture calls sin by the name of "thorn."

It would not be out of place to bring forward Zechariah, who was slain between the temple and the altar, as a witness to the incorrupt Mother. This Zechariah was a priest, and he also had the gift of prophecy. The power of his prophecy is recorded and proclaimed in the book of the Gospel. Divine grace prepared the way so that people would not think a birth from a virgin beyond belief, and it trained the unbelieving to assent by means of lesser wonders. A child is born to a woman who is barren and past her prime. This becomes a prelude to the mystery of the Virgin. Elizabeth did not become a mother by the power of nature, since she had grown old childless. Instead, the birth of the child is credited to the divine will. In the same way, the virgin's childbirth seems beyond belief, but it becomes believable when it is credited to God. So the child of the barren woman came before the birth from the virgin. Before he came into the light, he leapt in his mother's womb at the voice of the woman who was carrying the Lord. As soon as the forerunner of the Word was born, Zechariah's silence was broken by the breath of prophecy, and everything Zechariah then declared was a prophecy of what was to come. The prophetic Spirit led him by the hand to the knowledge of hidden things, and he understood the mystery of virginity in this incorrupt birth. So he did not shut the all-pure mother out of the place in the temple that the law had allotted to virgins. In this way he taught the Jews that the Creator of all things and King of all creation holds human nature, together with everything else, subject to himself. He leads it by his own will to whatever end he pleases and is not ruled by it, so it is in his power to fashion a new kind of birth that would not take away virginity from the woman who became a mother. For this reason he did not shut her out [Editorial notes, partly illegible: (19) "Of the incorrupt": [?] the manuscript read ἀφθ[?]... perhaps "of the ungrudging birth" [?]. (20) "The Creator of all" [?]...]

of the temple, from the place of the virgins. This place was the space between the temple and the altar. The Jews heard that the King of creation had come into human birth by the divine plan, and they feared becoming subject to a king. So they killed the man who bore witness to these things about the birth, sacrificing the priest at the very altar.

Why does the voice of the angels glorify the Godhead seen in the highest, saying, "Glory in the highest"? Because, it says, "and on earth peace." The angels were overjoyed at what had appeared: peace on earth. The earth was once cursed, bearing thorns and thistles [?]. It was a battlefield and a place of exile for the condemned. Now it has received peace. What a wonder! "Truth has sprung up from the earth." Such is the fruit that the earth of humankind has yielded. And these things happen because of God's good will among people. God is mingled with human nature so that what is human may be lifted up [?] together with the height of God.
